title: Bone Marrow Failure
subject: Medicine
summary: Bone marrow failure is the inability of the marrow to produce adequate blood cells, leading to pancytopenia. In low‑resource settings common causes include infections, nutritional deficiencies and inherited disorders. Recognising patterns, using limited investigations and initiating appropriate supportive care are key.

sections.p: Bone marrow failure describes a marked reduction in the production of red cells, white cells and platelets, confirmed by a hypocellular marrow on aspirate or biopsy.
b: Pancytopenia: Hb <10 g/dL, ANC <1.5 ×10⁹/L, platelets <100 ×10⁹/L
Marrow cellularity <30 % of normal for age

sections.p: Severity is graded by the depth of cytopenias and clinical impact.
b: Mild: Hb 8‑10 g/dL, ANC 1‑1.5 ×10⁹/L, platelets 80‑100 ×10⁹/L
Moderate: Hb 5‑8 g/dL, ANC 0.5‑1 ×10⁹/L, platelets 30‑80 ×10⁹/L
Severe: Hb <5 g/dL, ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L, platelets <30 ×10⁹/L

sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the most frequent aetiologies are infections, nutritional deficits and inherited disorders.
b: Infections: HIV, malaria, disseminated TB, hepatitis B/C, parvovirus B19
Nutritional: severe vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, copper deficiency
Inherited: sickle‑cell disease with aplastic crisis, Fanconi anaemia, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia
Drugs/toxins: chloramphenicol, benzene exposure, herbal remedies

sections.p: Patients present with symptoms of anaemia, infection and bleeding, often while already admitted for another condition.
b: Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, pallor
Fever, oral ulcers, recurrent infections
Petechiae, bruising, menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding

t.b: Confirms pancytopenia and guides urgency of treatment
Looks for abnormal cells (e.g., blasts, schistocytes) that suggest alternative diagnoses
Assesses cellularity and rules out infiltration (leukemia, lymphoma, myelofibrosis)

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B/C, parvovirus B19
t.b: Identifies treatable infectious causes
Detects nutritional deficiencies that mimic marrow failure

sections.p: Rapidly falling counts can precipitate life‑threatening events.
b: Severe neutropenia (<0.2 ×10⁹/L) → sepsis
Platelets <10 ×10⁹/L → intracranial haemorrhage
Hb <4 g/dL → high‑output cardiac failure

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and consider definitive therapy when resources allow.
b: Infection: broad‑spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic fever; antiretroviral therapy for HIV; anti‑TB drugs for disseminated TB
Transfusion: packed red cells for Hb <7 g/dL, platelets <20 ×10⁹/L with bleeding
Growth factors: filgrastim (G‑CSF) for severe neutropenia if available; otherwise monitor closely
Immunosuppression: antithymocyte globulin + cyclosporine for idiopathic aplastic anaemia when transplant not feasible
Definitive: allogeneic stem‑cell transplant in centres with capacity; otherwise long‑term supportive care

sections.p: Regular monitoring of counts and early treatment of infections prevent deterioration.
b: Weekly CBC until stable, then monthly
Vaccinate against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b and influenza
Counsel on avoidance of bone‑marrow toxic drugs and harmful herbal preparations

sections.p: Conditions that also cause pancytopenia but have different pathogenesis.
b: Acute leukemia – presence of blasts on smear, marrow hypercellular
Myelofibrosis – dry tap, teardrop RBCs, massive splenomegaly
Hypersplenism – enlarged spleen sequesters cells, marrow usually normal

sections.p: Certain laboratory patterns may mask the true problem.
b: Mildly low neutrophils in early HIV may be misread as viral suppression; repeat CBC after 2 weeks
Parvovirus B19 can cause isolated reticulocytopenia with normal WBC/platelets, mimicking early aplasia

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in haemoglobin >2 g/dL with haemodynamic instability

faq.q: Why is bone‑marrow cellularity compared to age?
faq.a: Normal marrow cellularity declines with age; using age‑adjusted norms avoids over‑diagnosing aplasia in older patients.
Severe malaria can suppress erythropoiesis and, in chronic infection, lead to pancytopenia.

faq.q: When is a stem‑cell transplant indicated?
faq.a: In young patients with severe aplastic anaemia who have a matched donor and access to transplant facilities.

exam: A 25‑year‑old with HIV presents with fever, Hb 6 g/dL, ANC 0.3 ×10⁹/L, platelets 25 ×10⁹/L – what is your immediate management? — Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics, give transfusion as indicated, and order marrow aspirate after stabilisation.

How does you differentiate aplastic anaemia from acute leukemia on peripheral smear? — Look for absence of blasts; aplasia shows normocytic normochromic RBCs and reduced granulocytes, whereas leukemia shows blasts >20 %.
Why is filgrastim preferred over steroids for neutropenic fever in marrow failure? — Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production without suppressing immunity; steroids can worsen infection risk.

A patient on long‑term chloramphenicol develops pancytopenia – what is the next step? — Discontinue chloramphenicol, monitor counts, and provide supportive transfusions; consider alternative antibiotics.
What laboratory test would you order first to rule out a reversible cause of marrow failure in a malnourished child? — Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels; deficiency is common and treatable.

Explain why splenomegaly suggests hypersplenism rather than primary marrow failure. — In hypersplenism the spleen sequesters cells, often with a palpable spleen; primary marrow failure usually has a normal‑sized spleen.

When is antithymocyte globulin indicated, and why avoid it in active infection? — Used for idiopathic aplastic anaemia when transplant unavailable; it further suppresses immunity, worsening infection.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden drop in Hb to 5 g/dL, reticulocytopenia and normal WBC – what is the likely cause? — Parvovirus B19‑induced aplastic crisis; treat with supportive transfusion and consider IVIG if severe.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam can differentiate primary marrow failure from secondary causes and identify life‑threatening complications.
b: Duration of cytopenia symptoms (weeks vs. acute days).
Recent infections (malaria, TB, HIV), drug exposures (chloramphenicol, benzene, herbal), radiation or chemotherapy.
Nutritional history (dietary restrictions, alcohol, vegetarianism, known B12/folate deficiency).
Family history of inherited marrow disorders (Fanconi anaemia, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, sickle‑cell disease).
Pregnancy status, recent childbirth, or lactation.
Bleeding history (menorrhagia, epistaxis, GI bleed, bruising).
Fever pattern, oral ulcers, skin lesions suggesting infection or drug reaction.

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, petechiae, ecchymoses, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly; presence suggests peripheral destruction or infiltrative disease, not isolated aplastic failure.
Assess for tachycardia, flow murmurs, signs of high‑output failure (wide pulse pressure); severe anaemia (<4 g/dL) often produces these findings.

t.a: Peripheral smear review at bedside (if microscope available)
t.b: Identify macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils (B12/folate deficiency) or blasts (leukemia); absence of blasts supports aplastic marrow but cannot rule out early leukemia.
Quick bedside estimate of platelet function; prolonged bleeding time may indicate qualitative platelet defect, not typical in pure aplastic failure.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Order tests that answer specific diagnostic questions; interpret using defined cut‑offs and have alternatives when resources are limited.
b: Complete blood count with differential – confirms pancytopenia and quantifies severity.
Reticulocyte count – low <2 % indicates production failure; high suggests peripheral loss.
Serum vitamin B12 and folate – low levels point to nutritional marrow suppression.
Serology for HIV, hepatitis B/C, parvovirus B19 – infections that can cause transient aplasia.
Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy – cellularity <30 % with fatty infiltration confirms aplastic anaemia; >20 % blasts suggests acute leukaemia.
Cytogenetics/FISH for PNH clone – detects paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, a common overlap.
Serum copper – deficiency can mimic aplasia; treatable.

t.b: Answers: Are all three lineages reduced?; Hb <10 g/dL, ANC <1.5 ×10⁹/L, platelets <100 ×10⁹/L define pancytopenia. Severity thresholds guide transfusion decisions.
Answers: Is marrow responding?; corrected retic <2 % supports production failure. If unavailable, use absolute retic count <50 ×10⁹/L as a proxy.
Answers: Is macrocytic anaemia due to deficiency?; <150 pmol/L is low. If assay unavailable, check methylmalonic acid or homocysteine if possible.
Answers: Is HIV‑associated marrow suppression present?; positive test prompts ART and opportunistic infection prophylaxis.
Answers: Is marrow hypocellular?; <30 % of normal for age confirms aplastic anaemia. Presence of >20 % blasts re‑classifies as acute leukaemia.
Answers: Is there an underlying PNH?; clone size >5 % is clinically relevant and may influence eculizumab eligibility.
Answers: Is copper deficiency present?; <0.8 µmol/L suggests deficiency; treat with copper sulphate if confirmed.

sections.p: Classification relies on marrow cellularity, cytopenia depth, and prognostic indices; severity guides transfusion and referral.
b: Aplastic anaemia – hypocellular marrow (<30 % cellularity) with pancytopenia and no blasts.
Mild aplasia – cytopenias above moderate thresholds, marrow cellularity 30‑50 %.
Secondary marrow failure – identified aetiology (infection, drug, nutritional) with otherwise similar laboratory profile.
Prognostic factors for poor response to immunosuppression: age >40 years, ANC <0.2 ×10⁹/L, and presence of cytogenetic abnormalities.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic aplastic marrow failure; careful clinical and laboratory discrimination is essential.

t.b: Points: dysplastic neutrophils, erythroid precursors, ring sideroblasts, cytopenias with marrow cellularity often >30 %. Cytogenetics help differentiate.
Points: splenomegaly, sequestration of cells, normal marrow cellularity. Ultrasound confirms splenomegaly; peripheral counts improve after splenectomy.
Points: hemolysis, dark urine, thrombosis, PNH clone on flow. Marrow may be hypocellular but hemolysis clues differentiate.
Points: macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils, low B12/folate, normal or mildly hypocellular marrow. Responds to replacement.
Points: temporal relation to offending drug, reversible after withdrawal. Bone marrow shows hypocellularity without dysplasia.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from immediate stabilisation to definitive therapy, ensuring safe escalation and appropriate referral in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen, IV fluids, and treat life‑threatening anaemia (Hb < 7 g/dL) with packed red cells.
3. Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic fever (ANC < 0.5 ×10⁹/L) after cultures; add antifungal if fever persists > 5 days.
4. Identify reversible cause: test for HIV, hepatitis, malaria, B12/folate, copper, parvovirus; treat the underlying infection or correct deficiency.
5. Supportive growth factors: give G‑CSF (filgrastim) for severe neutropenia when available; avoid steroids unless specific indication (e.g., adrenal insufficiency).

6. Consider disease‑specific definitive therapy: immunosuppression (ATG + cyclosporine) for aplastic anaemia without active infection; allogeneic stem‑cell transplant for severe aplastic anaemia in young patients with donor.
7. Monitor daily counts, reticulocyte response, renal/hepatic function; adjust transfusion thresholds and antibiotics based on trends.
8. Escalate or refer when: ANC < 0.2 ×10⁹/L with sepsis unresponsive to antibiotics, platelets < 10 ×10⁹/L with intracranial bleed, or when transplant is indicated and not available locally.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Awareness of adverse effects and drug interactions prevents iatrogenic worsening of marrow failure.
b: G‑CSF may cause bone pain; give analgesia and monitor for splenic enlargement – stop if splenomegaly > 2 cm develops.
ATG can precipitate serum sickness and viral reactivation; pre‑medicate with antihistamine, monitor CMV PCR, and give prophylactic antivirals if available.
Cyclosporine causes nephrotoxicity and hypertension; check serum creatinine and blood pressure weekly, avoid concomitant NSAIDs.
Broad‑spectrum beta‑lactams may cause neutropenia themselves; switch to narrower agents once cultures identify pathogen.
Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding but can increase thrombosis risk; avoid in patients with active thromboembolic disease.
Avoid chloramphenicol, benzene exposure, and unregulated herbal remedies as they can cause dose‑independent aplasia.

sections.p: Prompt recognition of life‑threatening sequelae guides timely referral to higher‑level care.
b: Platelet count < 10 ×10⁹/L with any intracranial or gastrointestinal bleed → emergent platelet transfusion, neurosurgical consult, and reversal of coagulopathy.
Hb < 4 g/dL or symptomatic high‑output cardiac failure → immediate packed red cell transfusion, cardiac monitoring, and consider exchange transfusion in sickle‑cell crisis.
Evidence of hemolysis (LDH > 2× ULN, indirect bilirubin > 2 mg/dL) with rising reticulocytes → evaluate for autoimmune hemolysis; start steroids if confirmed.
Progressive marrow hypocellularity on repeat biopsy despite therapy → refer for transplant evaluation or clinical trial enrolment.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, laboratory interpretation and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV: CD4 < 200 cells/µL predisposes to opportunistic infections; viral load guides ART timing; avoid live vaccines and consider prophylactic TMP‑SMX.
TB: Disseminated disease can cause marrow infiltration; obtain GeneXpert or culture; start anti‑TB therapy before immunosuppression if possible.
Malnutrition: B12/folate deficiency mimics marrow failure; measure serum levels, give high‑dose parenteral replacement, and re‑check counts after 7 days.
Pregnancy: Physiologic anaemia masks severity; use fetal‑safe antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone), avoid ATG unless life‑threatening, and transfuse with leukoreduced, irradiated products.
Diabetes: Hyperglycaemia worsens infection risk; monitor glucose during steroid use, adjust insulin, and avoid high‑dose steroids.
Alcohol & liver disease: Macrocytosis may be due to folate deficiency; correct folate, avoid hepatotoxic drugs, and use platelet thresholds of 50 ×10⁹/L for bleeding.
Renal failure: Reduces clearance of cyclosporine and ATG; dose‑adjust or select alternative immunosuppression; monitor electrolytes closely.
Age extremes: Neonates have higher physiological ANC; elderly have reduced marrow reserve and higher infection risk – lower threshold for transfusion and early referral.

sections.p: Tailored approaches respect physiological differences and resource constraints.
b: Children: Use weight‑based dosing for G‑CSF; consider bone‑marrow transplant earlier; avoid high‑dose cyclophosphamide; monitor growth parameters.
Pregnancy: Prioritise maternal stability; use irradiated, leukoreduced blood; defer ATG unless maternal life at risk; coordinate with obstetrics for delivery timing.
Elderly: Start with low‑intensity immunosuppression; avoid nephrotoxic cyclosporine if renal function impaired; set transfusion threshold Hb < 8 g/dL for symptomatic anaemia.
People with HIV: Initiate ART after stabilising infection; use G‑CSF cautiously as immune reconstitution may unmask infections; prophylaxis for PCP and MAC.

Low‑resource settings: Use bedside smear for reticulocyte count, simple malaria rapid test, and B12/folate kits; rely on irradiated, filtered blood; refer only when transplant is the only curative option.

3. A child on long‑term chloramphenicol develops pancytopenia. What is the immediate step and what long‑term monitoring is required?

6. A patient with severe neutropenia and persistent fever after 5 days of antibiotics – what next investigation and therapeutic change?

facts: Low reticulocyte count indicating production failure: <2 % of red cells.
Transfusion‑associated GVHD prevention: irradiate all cellular blood components (25 Gy).
Filgrastim (G‑CSF) indication: severe neutropenia (<0.5 ×10⁹/L) when growth factor is available.
Platelet transfusion threshold with active bleeding: <50 ×10⁹/L.
Common reversible causes to test first: vitamin B12, folate, copper, HIV, hepatitis B/C, malaria, parvovirus B19.

mnemonics.t: B = B12/folate deficiency, O = infections (HIV, TB, malaria), N = Nutritional copper deficiency, E = Exposures (benzene, chloramphenicol). Helps recall common reversible causes.

vivas.q: Define bone marrow failure and list its three main cytopenias.
vivas.a: Bone marrow failure is a marked reduction in production of red cells, white cells and platelets, resulting in pancytopenia (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).

vivas.q: What bedside history questions differentiate aplastic anaemia from acute leukemia?
vivas.a: Ask about rapid onset of symptoms, constitutional B‑symptoms, prior chemotherapy or toxin exposure, and family history of inherited marrow disorders; leukemia often has bone pain and lymphadenopathy.

vivas.q: How would you examine a patient for signs of bleeding risk?
vivas.a: Inspect for petechiae, ecchymoses, oral mucosal bleeding, and menorrhagia; palpate for splenomegaly; perform a tourniquet test for capillary fragility – a positive test suggests thrombocytopenia.

vivas.q: Interpret a peripheral smear showing pancytopenia with no blasts and a reticulocyte count of 1 %.
vivas.a: The low retic (<2 %) supports a production problem such as aplastic anaemia rather than peripheral destruction.

vivas.q: Why is irradiation of blood products mandatory before transfusing an immunocompromised marrow transplant recipient?
vivas.a: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes, preventing transfusion‑associated graft‑versus‑host disease, which is fatal in immunocompromised patients.

vivas.q: What is the first laboratory test to rule out a reversible cause of marrow failure in a malnourished adult?
vivas.a: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels; low values point to nutritional deficiency that can be corrected.

vivas.q: How do you distinguish drug‑induced neutropenia from ineffective granulopoiesis on bone‑marrow biopsy?
vivas.a: Drug‑induced neutropenia shows a hypocellular marrow with normal maturation; ineffective granulopoiesis shows dysplastic precursors and increased apoptosis.

vivas.q: When is antithymocyte globulin (ATG) indicated in aplastic anaemia and why avoid it in active infection?
vivas.a: ATG is used for severe aplastic anaemia when a matched donor is unavailable; it suppresses T‑cell mediated marrow destruction but worsens infection risk, so active infection must be treated first.

vivas.q: Explain why splenomegaly suggests hypersplenism rather than primary marrow failure.
vivas.a: Splenomegaly indicates sequestration and destruction of blood cells; primary marrow failure typically has a small or normal spleen.

vivas.q: What is the management priority for a patient with Hb 4 g/dL, ANC 0.2 ×10⁹/L and platelets 20 ×10⁹/L presenting with fever?
vivas.a: Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics immediately, give packed red cells (Hb < 7 g/dL) and platelet transfusion (threshold < 50 ×10⁹/L with fever), then investigate reversible causes.

vivas.q: Why are steroids avoided in neutropenic fever unless a specific indication exists?
vivas.a: Steroids further suppress immune function and can mask infection signs, increasing mortality; they are only used for conditions like adrenal insufficiency or specific inflammatory diseases.

vivas.q: Which staining method is preferred for air‑dry smears because it highlights cytoplasm?
vivas.a: May‑Grünwald‑Giemsa (MGG) stain, used for peripheral blood films and marrow smears.

vivas.q: What is the fundamental nature of circulating myeloblasts, myelocytes and granulocytes with marrow proliferation?
vivas.a: They represent a myeloproliferative neoplasm, most commonly chronic myeloid leukaemia.

vivas.q: Which intervention specifically stimulates neutrophil production in drug‑induced neutropenia?
What pathological marrow finding distinguishes ineffective granulopoiesis from drug‑suppressive neutropenia?
vivas.a: Dysplastic changes in myeloid precursors (e.g., hypogranular neutrophils) indicate ineffective granulopoiesis; a uniformly hypocellular marrow without dysplasia suggests drug suppression.

vivas.q: What is the most common extranodal site for non‑Hodgkin lymphoma after bone marrow?
Name the genetic disorder with defective DNA interstrand cross‑link repair causing progressive marrow failure.
Describe compensatory mechanisms in chronic haemolytic anaemia and their effect on marrow and radiographs.
vivas.a: Increased erythropoietin drives marrow hyperplasia, leading to expanded marrow spaces and ‘hair‑on‑end’ periosteal reaction on long‑bone X‑rays.

vivas.q: Outline the typical peripheral‑blood and marrow findings in myelodysplastic syndrome.
vivas.a: Cytopenias with dysplastic erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic lines; ringed sideroblasts may be present; marrow cellularity is often hypercellular with ≥10 % blasts.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever, Hb 6 g/dL, ANC 0.3 ×10⁹/L, platelets 25 ×10⁹/L. Which immediate step is most appropriate?
o: Give packed red cells, platelets and broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics
Observe and repeat counts in 48 h
mcqs.e: Severe cytopenias with fever require antibiotics and transfusion support immediately.

mcqs.q: Which modification of blood products prevents transfusion‑associated GVHD?
mcqs.e: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes, the only proven method to prevent TA‑GVHD.

mcqs.q: Which stain is chosen for air‑dry marrow smears because it highlights cytoplasm well?
mcqs.e: May‑Grünwald‑Giemsa stains cytoplasm intensely on air‑dry preparations.

mcqs.q: A patient on long‑term chloramphenicol develops pancytopenia. What is the next step?
o: Stop chloramphenicol and give supportive transfusions
mcqs.e: Drug‑induced marrow suppression is reversible; stop the offending drug and provide supportive care.

mcqs.q: In a patient with active bleeding, the platelet transfusion threshold is:
mcqs.e: Guidelines recommend transfusing when platelets are <50 ×10⁹/L with active bleeding.

mcqs.q: Which finding on marrow biopsy distinguishes ineffective granulopoiesis from pure drug‑suppressed neutropenia?
mcqs.e: Dysplastic granulocytic precursors indicate ineffective granulopoiesis, not simple suppression.

cases.v: A 24‑year‑old woman with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden Hb drop to 5 g/dL, reticulocyte count 1 %, no fever, and platelets 120 ×10⁹/L.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
qs.a: Aplastic (parvovirus B19) crisis causing red‑cell aplasia.

qs.q: Which immediate investigation should be ordered?
qs.a: Serum parvovirus B19 PCR or IgM and a repeat reticulocyte count.
Supportive transfusion of packed red cells and, if confirmed, give IV immunoglobulin.

cases.v: A 55‑year‑old man from a rural clinic presents with fever, weight loss, pancytopenia (Hb 7 g/dL, ANC 0.4 ×10⁹/L, platelets 30 ×10⁹/L) and splenomegaly 4 cm below costal margin.

qs.q: What differential diagnoses should be considered?
qs.a: Aplastic anaemia, acute leukaemia, myelofibrosis, hypersplenism secondary to malaria or TB.

qs.q: Which bedside test helps distinguish hypersplenism from primary marrow failure?
qs.a: Examination for splenomegaly; a markedly enlarged spleen suggests sequestration rather than pure marrow failure.

qs.q: What is the next diagnostic step in a low‑resource setting?
qs.a: Perform a peripheral smear and, if possible, a bone‑marrow aspirate; if unavailable, send a sample to a referral lab for morphology and cytogenetics.

mistakes: Confusing the low reticulocyte threshold (<1 %) with the correct <2 % for production failure.
Using the wrong platelet transfusion threshold for active bleeding (20 ×10⁹/L instead of 50 ×10⁹/L).
Stating filgrastim is preferred over steroids for neutropenic fever; steroids are generally avoided.
Describing aplastic anaemia peripheral smear as having ‘normocellular blasts’; it shows few or no blasts.
Applying the Camitta criteria to predict immunosuppression response rather than severity grading.
Citing >20 % lymphoblasts as the ALL cut‑off; the correct threshold is >25 %.
